passage: The corridor outside the staff room was full of waiting families on parent-teacher day. Lalit sat on the bench with his bag on his knees while other children whispered. Through the half-open door he caught fragments: “the fees after March...” and his father Vishal's low voice, “Please don't say it in front of the boy.” His mother studied the noticeboard as though it were a map. In the car, Vishal talked about traffic. Lalit asked, “Was everything fine?” “Nothing to worry about,” Vishal said, too quickly. Lalit stared out of the window and thought of being pulled out of school, or of somebody being ill. The class teacher waved from the gate.

qa.q: What fragment did Lalit catch through the half-open door?
qa.a: He caught “the fees after March...” through the half-open door.

qa.q: What might Lalit be worried about as he stares out of the window?
qa.a: Lalit worries about being pulled out of school or somebody being ill. Not knowing leaves him guessing at something worse than the truth may be.

qa.q: How could Vishal or Lalit's mother respond so Lalit worries less?
qa.a: They could give Lalit a short, calm, honest explanation of what he needs to know and invite his questions, instead of saying “Nothing to worry about” too quickly.

qa.q: Why might Vishal say “Nothing to worry about” so quickly?
qa.a: Vishal is probably trying to shield his son from a money worry, though the quick answer leaves Lalit anxious.

grounding: A teenager overhears fragments at school, senses an unspoken family matter and imagines worse than the truth.

passage:
Dear Jeevan bhaiya,
I'm writing because I can't say this out loud at home. Ammi and Abbu whisper in the kitchen after every phone call, and they stop when I walk in. There is a brown envelope in Ammi's cupboard that wasn't there in the winter. Nani's visits stopped, and nobody says why. When I asked, Ammi said, “Study, beta.” I have started thinking of terrible things: that someone is very ill, or that we are in some kind of trouble. I keep watching Ammi's face at dinner to work out which. If you know anything, tell me, or tell me to stop guessing.
Rehana

qa.q: Where did Rehana find a brown envelope?
qa.a: There is a brown envelope in Ammi's cupboard.

qa.q: What is Rehana worried about when watching Ammi's face at dinner?
qa.a: Rehana fears something terrible, such as an illness or trouble, and is trying to read Ammi's face for clues.

qa.q: What could Rehana do besides guessing?
qa.a: Rehana could ask Ammi or Abbu directly and gently whether something is worrying them, and say that not knowing is hard.

qa.q: What might Ammi be trying to do by saying, “Study, beta”?
qa.a: Ammi may be trying to protect the child from a worry and keep home steady, without seeing that the silence is making it worse.

grounding: A teenager senses something undiscussed at home, guesses at terrible explanations and watches Ammi closely.

passage: Usha, you know your friend Zainab notices everything, right? So for three weeks now, whenever I walk into the kitchen, Ammi and Khala stop talking. Abbu takes phone calls on the stairs and comes back with his face grey. Yesterday Ammi said we're skipping the trip to Lucknow this year, 'just because'. Nobody says anything else. At night I lie awake making up stories. First I thought Abbu lost his job. Then I thought, what if he's ill and they're hiding it? Last night I even checked his medicine drawer. Nothing. Honestly, not knowing is worse than any bad news could be. My little brother just watches cartoons; he has no idea. Do you think I should ask them straight out?

qa.q: What did Ammi say about the trip to Lucknow?
qa.a: That they are skipping it this year, 'just because'.

qa.q: What is Zainab feeling while lying awake at night?
qa.a: Zainab feels anxious and restless, imagining worse and worse reasons, even checking Abbu's medicine drawer.

qa.q: What would you advise Zainab to do?
qa.a: Pick a calm moment and gently ask Ammi what is going on, saying that the silence is causing more worry than the truth might.

qa.q: How might Abbu be feeling as he takes calls on the stairs?
qa.a: He seems strained and worried, with his face grey, perhaps trying to keep a problem away from the children without knowing Zainab has noticed.

grounding: A teenager notices a family silence and, left without an explanation, imagines reasons worse than the likely truth.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: My name is Madhuri, and I'm the one in our family who notices things. Jagdish Chacha visits us every Diwali but never stays the night. When he comes, Dadi gets up and goes to her room. Papa talks to him in a too-cheerful voice, and the photo album with the old Kanpur house is always put away before he arrives. This year he held my little brother on his lap, and his hands shook a bit. When I asked Mummy why Dadi leaves, she said, 'Grown-up matters.' Since then I've invented a dozen stories: prison, a fight about land, something worse. I watch Chacha's face at dinner, and I can't tell if he is sad, or ashamed, or just tired.

qa.q: What happens to the photo album before Jagdish Chacha arrives?
qa.a: The album with the old Kanpur house is always put away.

qa.q: What is Madhuri feeling after Mummy says 'Grown-up matters'?
qa.a: Madhuri feels anxious and restless with curiosity, inventing a dozen stories, some of them frightening, like prison.

qa.q: What small step could Madhuri's parents take?
qa.a: Share a simple, honest version of the story, so Madhuri isn't left imagining something worse than the truth.

qa.q: What might it be like for Jagdish Chacha during these visits?
qa.a: He may feel unwelcome and uneasy, with Dadi leaving the room and Papa's voice too cheerful; his shaking hands hint that he feels it.

grounding: A teenager watches a relative who is never discussed and fills the family's silence with frightening guesses.

passage: Sunday: Neelam heard Ammi on the phone say 'the reports' and then shut the door. Her brother Rafiq kept playing his game, but Neelam stood outside in the corridor for a long minute. Wednesday: Ammi's eyes were red at breakfast. Abbu drove her somewhere and called it 'bank work'. Neelam couldn't focus in chemistry; she had already decided Ammi had something terrible and nobody would tell her. The next Monday: Ammi sat both of them down. 'Nanu has a heart problem. The doctors are treating it. I was scared, so I kept quiet. I'm sorry.' Neelam cried, but her shoulders loosened. It was bad news, but it was smaller than the one she had built in her head.

qa.q: What did Abbu call the trip he took Ammi on, on Wednesday?
qa.a: He called it 'bank work'.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling in chemistry class on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was anxious and frightened, convinced Ammi had something terrible and that nobody would tell her.

qa.q: What did Ammi finally do that helped, and what could have helped sooner?
qa.a: She sat both children down and explained about Nanu honestly; a short, honest word earlier would have spared Neelam days of imagining worse.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have experienced the same week?
qa.a: Rafiq kept playing his game and may not have noticed much, so Monday's talk might have come as more of a shock to him.

grounding: Over several days a teenager senses an unspoken family worry, imagines the worst, and is relieved when told the smaller truth.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage:
Vishal, you keep asking why nobody talks about Chhote Mama. Let your Urmila mausi tell you what it was like when I was fifteen.
For a whole year our house had sudden silences. Your nani would hang up the phone when I walked in. Nanaji stopped going to his evening walks with friends. I made up stories in my head: that we were poor, that someone was dying, that Nanaji had done something terrible. I was so anxious I couldn't sleep; I listened at doors.
One night I finally asked your nani straight out. She was quiet for a long time, then sat me down. Chhote Mama had borrowed money from the wrong people, and Nanaji was quietly paying it back. That was all. Nobody was dying.
She said, "We thought we were protecting you."
I told her, "Not knowing was worse."

qa.q: What did Nani do when Urmila walked in during a phone call?
qa.a: She would hang up the phone.

qa.q: How did young Urmila feel during that year?
qa.a: She was anxious and sleepless, imagining things far worse than the truth, like someone dying.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what does it suggest about family secrets?
qa.a: Urmila asking Nani straight out; hearing the real, smaller truth ended a year of frightening guesses.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt when Urmila asked her straight out?
qa.a: Nani was likely torn, having kept the secret to protect Urmila, and perhaps relieved to finally share it.

grounding: Shows a teenager sensing an unspoken family problem and imagining far worse than the truth until it is finally explained.
